strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed appearance addresses a useful gap between image-only and text-only retrieval. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery assembled from three source datasets.
The reported improvements are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for feature averaging using the same fine-tuned encoders.

The two-stage framework is technically coherent and practical. It learns composition without CPR triplet supervision, reuses existing person image-caption annotations, and requires only a small mapping network after encoder fine-tuning.

The experiments include useful ablations of supervision, training-data quantity and source, network architecture, and fusion. Table 2 provides partial controlled evidence for the proposed objectives. Training settings and supplementary runtime measurements also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline comparison with Pic2Word is confounded. Table 1 explicitly states that its inversion network was trained with the original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This creates a representation mismatch that disadvantages the baseline. Table 2 partially addresses the issue, but a fully retrained, matched-backbone Pic2Word comparison and evaluation of the closely related textual-inversion method cited as [2] are needed to establish the claimed advantage.

Methodological originality is limited and insufficiently distinguished from prior work. Mapping image embeddings into pseudo-word tokens already underlies Pic2Word and related methods, while the encoder fine-tuning and matching losses reuse established techniques. The main contribution appears to be the person-specific task, benchmark, and adaptation; the manuscript overstates the novelty of the underlying framework.

Model selection is insufficiently separated from final evaluation. ITCPR is described exclusively as a test set, yet Appendices C.3-C.5 identify optimal architectures and fusion configurations using its results. No independent CPR validation procedure is described, making the optimized results potentially optimistic. Missing uncertainty estimates particularly weaken conclusions about small fusion gains.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the defining identity-preservation requirement. Image-only baselines use CLIP rather than specialized clothes-changing person retrieval models. Because dataset construction favors partially shared clothing, aggregate scores cannot establish how reliably the method preserves identity beyond residual appearance cues. Comparisons with appropriate identity-focused baselines, appearance-matched distractors, and results separated by source dataset would strengthen the task-level claims.

The benchmark needs stronger annotation documentation and validation. Appendix B.1 searches an unspecified top-k neighborhood before manually adding positives, but does not report screening coverage, annotator agreement, or an audit for positives outside that neighborhood. Detailed relevance rules and reproducible query/gallery manifests are especially important because this new benchmark supplies all CPR evaluation evidence.

The manuscript explicitly motivates surveillance and public-security applications but does not discuss privacy, consent, source-dataset reuse and redistribution permissions, or consequences of misidentification. These are relevant omissions for a proposed release involving identifiable people, although the manuscript alone does not establish an actual ethical violation.
